passage:
Four months after Eshaan's sister Pooja died, the office had gone back to normal. People asked about the quarterly report, not about her.
Chinmay didn't. On Monday he stopped at Eshaan's desk with two steel boxes. "My mother made extra aloo paratha. Lunch on the terrace?"
Up there, he asked, "How are you today? Not in general. Today."
Eshaan shrugged. "Today's okay. Yesterday was bad. Her birthday's next week."
"Pooja would've made us all wear party hats," Chinmay said, and Eshaan laughed, surprised.
"Nobody says her name anymore. It's like she got deleted."
"Then I'll keep saying it. And Thursday, a walk after work? Same as last Thursday."
Eshaan nodded, tearing the paratha slowly. It wasn't a big thing. It was the fourth Thursday in a row.

qa.q: What did Chinmay bring to Eshaan's desk on Monday?
qa.a: Two steel boxes of extra aloo paratha his mother made.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan laugh, surprised, when Chinmay mentioned party hats?
qa.a: After months of nobody saying Pooja's name, hearing it with a warm memory felt like a relief to Eshaan, who felt she had been 'deleted'.

qa.q: What makes Chinmay's support work at this stage?
qa.a: It is small and steady: asking about today, saying Pooja's name and keeping a Thursday walk going months later, when others have moved on.

qa.q: What might the office going back to normal feel like for Eshaan?
qa.a: It can feel as if Pooja has been forgotten, which leaves Eshaan lonelier in grief even while work carries on.

grounding: Shows a friend giving ongoing, ordinary presence months after a loss by saying the lost person's name, sharing meals and walks, and asking about today.

passage:
Dear Elizabeth,
I know it's been seven months since your mum Margaret died, and I know most people have stopped asking. I haven't stopped thinking about her. Yesterday I passed the bakery where she always bought those awful coconut buns, and I laughed out loud remembering her defending them.
I'm not writing to ask how you are "in general". I'm asking how today is. Just today. You can answer in one word.
I'm making biryani on Saturday, far too much as usual. Can I bring a box over? Or would you rather come for a walk by the canal on Sunday morning? Or both. Or neither, and I'll ask again in two weeks.
No need to reply quickly.
With love,
Salma

qa.q: Where did Salma offer to walk with Elizabeth?
qa.a: By the canal on Sunday morning.

qa.q: Why does Salma tell Elizabeth about the coconut buns?
qa.a: Salma fondly remembers Margaret and wants Elizabeth to know Margaret is still thought of and talked about, even though most people have stopped asking. 🤍

qa.q: What makes Salma's offer easy for Elizabeth to accept or turn down?
qa.a: It offers small choices, a box of biryani, a walk, both or neither, promises to ask again in two weeks, and says there is no need to reply quickly.

qa.q: What might it be like for Elizabeth to receive this letter seven months on?
qa.a: Elizabeth may feel less alone hearing Margaret's name and a funny memory, and relieved to be asked only about today.

grounding: Illustrates a friend's ongoing presence months after a death: naming the lost person, offering a meal or walk, and asking about today.

passage:
People ask me what you do when a friend loses a parent. I'm Joseph, and I got it wrong for a while.
When Samir's mother died in January, I was there for the funeral. Then, like everyone, I went back to normal. I didn't mention her. I thought I was being kind.
In April, Samir said, "Everyone's forgotten her." That hit me.
So I changed. I started saying her name. "Your Ammi would've hated this movie." Every few weeks I'd text, "Walk tonight?" or bring biryani over. I'd ask, "How are you today?" not "How are you?"
It's not a big gesture. It's just showing up again and again. And he talks about her now. Laughs about her, even.

qa.q: When did Samir's mother die?
qa.a: In January.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when Samir said "Everyone's forgotten her"?
qa.a: Joseph felt shaken and regretful, realising the silence had hurt instead of helped.

qa.q: What changed in Joseph's approach, and why does it work?
qa.a: Joseph started saying her name and offering walks and meals over months, because steady presence matters more than one big gesture.

qa.q: What is it like for Samir now that Joseph keeps showing up?
qa.a: Samir seems less alone, able to talk and even laugh about his Ammi.

grounding: Shows a friend learning to keep saying a lost mother's name and offering walks and meals months later, showing up again and again.

passage:
I work at the same bank branch as Leela and Chinmay, so I noticed this over the months.
Chinmay's father died in February. Everyone sent flowers. By April, nobody mentioned it.
Except Leela. Every few weeks she'd put a steel tiffin on his desk: "Aunty's recipe, try it." Once, in July, I heard her say, "Your dad would have loved this rain, na? He used to talk about it." Chinmay went still, then smiled.
She asked him things like, "How are you today?" Not "How are you?" The difference seemed small. But I saw Chinmay start to stay back after work and talk to her.
I can't say what went on inside him. But Leela kept showing up, and he kept opening up.

qa.q: When did Chinmay's father die?
qa.a: In February.

qa.q: What might Leela have been feeling when she mentioned Chinmay's dad and the rain?
qa.a: She was probably caring and a bit careful, wanting to keep his father's memory alive without upsetting him.

qa.q: What did Leela do that made a difference?
qa.a: She kept showing up for months, with tiffins, his father's name and "How are you today?", instead of one big gesture.

qa.q: What was it like for Chinmay when Leela mentioned his dad?
qa.a: Chinmay went still and then smiled, suggesting he felt touched and relieved that someone remembered.

grounding: Shows a colleague watching a friend support a mourner for months by saying his father's name, bringing food and asking how he is today.

passage:
March: Binita's brother died in a road accident. Anirban came to the cremation, then to the house every evening for a week, sitting mostly in silence.
June: Everyone else had gone quiet. Anirban texted: "Thinking of Rohan today. Walk by the lake Sunday?" They walked for an hour. Binita talked about Rohan's awful jokes. Anirban laughed at all of them.
November: On Rohan's birthday, Anirban brought mutton roll, Rohan's favourite, and two cups of tea. "How are you today?" he asked. Binita cried, then ate a roll, then said, "You're the only one who still says his name."

qa.q: What did Anirban bring on Rohan's birthday?
qa.a: Mutton roll, Rohan's favourite, and two cups of tea.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when she said Anirban was the only one who still said his name?
qa.a: She felt grateful and moved, but also alone, since others had stopped mentioning Rohan.

qa.q: Why was Anirban's support effective over the months?
qa.a: He kept showing up with walks, food and Rohan's name long after others went quiet, offering steady presence.

qa.q: What might Anirban be experiencing on those visits?
qa.a: Anirban is probably sad for Binita but determined to be there, and maybe glad to laugh at Rohan's jokes with her.

grounding: Shows a friend supporting a mourner over months with walks, food, the lost brother's name and "How are you today?".

passage: "Come, sit with your Pooja Nani while the dal cooks. You asked how to help your friend whose brother died. When I was twenty-five, my dear friend Kamal lost his young wife, Leela. At the funeral, everyone came. Three months later, nobody came. People were afraid to say her name, as if it would break him. So I did a small thing. Every Thursday I went with a tiffin, and I said her name. 'Leela loved this pickle.' 'Leela would laugh at this.' The first time, his eyes filled. By the fifth Thursday he was telling me Leela stories himself. Some weeks we only walked to the lake and back. And I always asked, 'How are you today?' Not in general. Today. It was never one big thing, beta. It was showing up."

qa.q: On which day did Pooja go to Kamal with a tiffin?
qa.a: Every Thursday.

qa.q: Why did Pooja keep saying Leela's name?
qa.a: She was sad to see Kamal left alone and hoped hearing the name would show him Leela was still remembered.

qa.q: What choice by young Pooja made the difference?
qa.a: Choosing steady small visits, saying Leela's name and asking how he was that day, instead of one big gesture.

qa.q: How did the Thursdays change things for Kamal?
qa.a: Kamal went from tearing up to telling Leela stories himself, likely feeling less alone in his grief.

grounding: Shows a friend who keeps saying the lost person's name, brings meals and walks for months and asks how the mourner is today.
